name: Glaucoma
preview_text: Sudden throbbing pain, dull ache, or stabbing pain - each type of glaucoma discomfort points to a different TCM pattern. With consistent herbs and acupuncture, many patients see a ...
synonyms: ["Optic Nerve Damage", "Hemorrhagic Glaucoma", "Bleeding Glaucoma", "Blood-filled Eye", "Haemorrhagic Glaucoma"]
conventional_description: Glaucoma is a group of eye conditions that damage the optic nerve, often associated with elevated intraocular pressure. It is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The most common form, primary open-angle glaucoma, develops slowly and painlessly, gradually reducing peripheral vision. Acute angle-closure glaucoma can cause sudden, severe eye pain, headache, nausea, and blurred vision, and is a medical emergency. Diagnosis involves measuring eye pressure, examining the optic nerve, and testing the visual field.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment aims to lower eye pressure to prevent further optic nerve damage. This is typically achieved through prescription eye drops (prostaglandin analogs, beta-blockers, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), oral medications, laser treatments (trabeculoplasty, iridotomy), or surgery (trabeculectomy, drainage implants). The goal is to manage, not cure, the condition, often requiring lifelong treatment and monitoring.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the eye is intimately connected to the Liver and Kidney organ systems. The Liver opens into the eyes, so any disturbance in Liver function - especially stagnation or heat - can directly affect vision and eye pressure. The Kidney stores the essence that nourishes the eyes, and when this essence is depleted, the eye tissues lose their resilience and function. This is why glaucoma is never just a local eye problem; it's a reflection of deeper imbalances.
When intense anger, stress, or frustration stirs up Liver Fire, it blazes upward along the Liver channel into the eyes, causing a sudden, painful spike in pressure - what TCM calls the 'green wind' (绿风) pattern. This is a classic excess condition: the eye is red, hard, and throbbing, and the person may be irritable with a bitter taste in the mouth. It's the TCM equivalent of an acute angle-closure attack.
In many chronic cases, the root is a deficiency. Overwork, aging, insufficient sleep, or prolonged illness deplete the Yin fluids of the Kidney and Liver. Without enough Yin to anchor it, a subtle heat rises, drying and damaging the eye. This leads to the slow, insidious vision loss and dull ache of open-angle glaucoma. The tongue is often red with cracks, and the pulse feels thin and rapid.
Finally, when Qi and Blood fail to flow smoothly through the delicate channels of the eye - often after repeated acute episodes or in long-standing disease - stagnation sets in. This creates a fixed, stabbing pain and dark spots that don't move. The optic nerve becomes starved of nourishment. This pattern is less common but important, as it requires moving the blood to restore circulation.
classical_quote: 「绿风内障，初患时头旋，两额角相牵瞳人，连鼻鬲皆痛，或时红白花起……此是肝肺之劳，或时脑痛，兼无翳膜，瞳人开大青绿色。」
classical_translation: "In Green Wind Internal Obstruction, at the onset there is dizziness, pain in the temples pulling toward the pupil, pain connecting to the nose, and sometimes red or white halos appear. … This is due to overstrain of the Liver and Lung, sometimes with headache. There is no nebula, but the pupil is dilated and shows a bluish-green color."

tcm_diagnosis:
To differentiate patterns in glaucoma, a TCM practitioner begins by asking about the speed of onset and the nature of the eye pain. A sudden, violent attack with intense throbbing pain, redness, and nausea points strongly toward Liver Fire Blazing (肝火上炎, gān huǒ shàng yán). This acute pattern feels like a firestorm in the eye, and the person often describes the pain as unbearable, with a sharp loss of vision.
If the condition has been smoldering for months or years, with a dull ache, dry eyes, and gradually blurring vision, the root is more likely Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency (肝肾阴虚, gān shèn yīn xū). The eye lacks the cooling, moistening nourishment of Yin, so symptoms worsen with overwork or late nights. The tongue is often red with little coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid.
When the pain is stabbing rather than throbbing, and the person sees fixed dark spots or shadows that do not move, Qi and Blood Stagnation (气血瘀阻, qì xuè yū zǔ) is the key pattern. This often develops after repeated acute attacks or in long-standing glaucoma, where the channels of the eye become obstructed. The tongue may appear dark or have purple spots, and the pulse feels choppy or wiry.
During the examination, a practitioner will also note the color of the eye and the tension of the eyeball. A fiery red eye with a rock-hard globe is typical of Liver Fire, while a pale, dry eye with normal or only slightly elevated pressure suggests Yin Deficiency. A history of trauma or chronic disease that leads to stasis can help confirm the stagnation pattern.

patterns.symptoms: ["Sudden, intense throbbing eye pain", "Red, swollen, or burning eyes", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Intense irritability and short temper", "Throbbing headache at the temples or crown", "Constipation and dark yellow urine"]
patterns.worse_with: Anger and frustration, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Alcohol, Hot weather or environments, Excessive screen time and eye strain
patterns.better_with: Cool compress over the eyes, Rest in a dark, quiet room, Chrysanthemum or peppermint tea, Gentle eye exercises and breaks
patterns.why_this_happens: Intense anger, frustration, or prolonged stress cause Liver Qi to stagnate and quickly transform into Fire. This blazing Fire surges upward along the Liver channel directly into the eyes, obstructing the normal flow of fluids and Qi within the eye. The result is a sudden, dangerous spike in intraocular pressure, along with sharp pain, redness, and blurred vision.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, dry yellow coating, possible red prickles. Pulse: wiry, rapid, full and forceful.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and stress directly stagnate Liver Qi and transform it into Fire, which is the root mechanism of this acute glaucoma pattern. Cooling foods, compresses, and quiet environments help drain that Heat and calm the upward surging Qi, while rest and gentle movement prevent further agitation of the Liver.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add Heat. Favor cooling foods like cucumber, celery, chrysanthemum tea, and mung beans. Prioritize stress management through gentle walks, deep breathing, or meditation, and take frequent breaks from screens to rest the eyes.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry, gritty eyes with a dull ache", "Blurred vision that worsens with overuse and fatigue", "Night sweats and heat in the palms, soles, and chest", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees", "Dizziness and ringing in the ears"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and chronic fatigue, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Excessive screen time and eye strain, Stress and emotional tension, Late nights and insufficient sleep
patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep and early nights, Cool, humidified environment, Moistening foods like pears and bone broth, Gentle eye rest and palming
patterns.why_this_happens: The eyes are deeply connected to the Liver and Kidneys. When the Yin fluids of these organs become depleted over time, the eyes lose their natural lubrication and nourishment. This leads to chronic dryness, a dull ache, and blurred vision. The underlying deficiency also allows a subtle heat to rise, which can slowly increase pressure inside the eye and damage the optic nerve.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and wiry, especially weak at the left Chi (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Liver Yin are the body's cooling, moistening reserves. Activities that burn the candle at both ends, like late nights, overwork, and prolonged mental focus, directly consume these fluids. Spicy and fried foods add heat that further dries up Yin. Rest, hydration, and nourishing foods help replenish these deep reserves, cooling the subtle heat that rises to the eyes and allowing the optic nerve to be properly nourished.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid late nights, as sleep is when the body rebuilds Yin. Keep your environment slightly cool and use a humidifier if the air is dry. Eat moistening foods like pears, black sesame, goji berries, and bone broths. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Take frequent breaks from screens and practice gentle eye exercises to prevent strain.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and Blood fail to flow smoothly through the delicate channels of the eye, stagnation sets in. This obstruction acts like a dam, causing pressure to build and producing a fixed, stabbing pain deep within the eye. Over time, the lack of fresh, nourishing Blood reaching the optic nerve leads to irreversible dark spots in the vision and gradual sight loss.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a knife scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood Stagnation is like a frozen river: cold and stillness make it worse, while warmth, gentle movement, and emotional ease help it flow again. Anger knots the Liver Qi, which is the primary driver of Blood circulation, so calming the mind and moving the body directly address the root of the stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the body warm and the circulation active with daily gentle exercise like walking or tai chi. Eat small amounts of blood-moving spices such as turmeric, ginger, and a little saffron, and include dark leafy greens. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can congeal Blood. Protect your eyes from prolonged screen time and emotional stress that tightens Qi flow.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really lower eye pressure?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help reduce intraocular pressure, especially when combined with herbal medicine. Points around the eye and on the Liver and Kidney channels work to calm rising heat, nourish Yin, and improve local circulation. While not a replacement for emergency medication during an acute attack, regular acupuncture has been shown in some studies to produce a modest but meaningful drop in pressure and may help stabilize fluctuations.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine Chinese herbs with my glaucoma eye drops?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but it must be done under professional supervision. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your ophthalmologist about all medications and herbs you are taking. Certain herbs that move blood could theoretically interact with blood-thinning medications, and some herbs may lower systemic blood pressure. Never stop your prescribed eye drops without consulting your eye doctor, as sudden discontinuation can cause a dangerous pressure spike.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: For chronic glaucoma, a typical initial course is weekly sessions for 6-8 weeks. After that, frequency may reduce to every other week or monthly, depending on how your pressure and symptoms respond. Acute attacks may require more intensive treatment. Many patients continue with maintenance sessions long-term to support eye health.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have glaucoma?
faqs.answer: To prevent stirring up Liver Fire, avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods, as well as alcohol and excessive caffeine. Very cold or raw foods can weaken digestion and create dampness, which may contribute to stagnation. Instead, focus on moistening, cooling foods like pears, goji berries, and leafy greens. See the Diet section for more details.

faqs.question: Will TCM cure my glaucoma?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to manage and stabilize glaucoma by correcting the underlying imbalances that contribute to nerve damage and pressure elevation. While it may not 'cure' the structural changes already present, many patients find that with consistent treatment, their vision stabilizes and they can reduce their reliance on medications or delay surgery. The goal is to preserve the optic nerve and prevent further loss.

faqs.question: I have normal-tension glaucoma - can TCM help?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In fact, normal-tension glaucoma is often a perfect fit for TCM because the damage is happening without high pressure, suggesting a deficiency or stagnation pattern that Western medicine doesn't address. Nourishing Kidney and Liver Yin or moving stagnant Blood can improve microcirculation and nerve nutrition, potentially slowing progression.

research.title: Acupuncture for glaucoma
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review assessing the effectiveness of acupuncture compared with other treatments, no treatment, or sham acupuncture for glaucoma. The review included one small trial and found insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about its efficacy in reducing intraocular pressure or preventing visual field loss.
research.periodical: Law SK, Li T. Acupuncture for glaucoma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2013, Issue 5. Art. No.: CD006030.

research.title: Effect of acupuncture on intraocular pressure in glaucoma patients: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: A pilot RCT that compared true acupuncture to sham acupuncture in 22 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma. The true acupuncture group showed a statistically significant reduction in intraocular pressure immediately after treatment, though the effect was transient.
research.periodical: Takayama S, Seki T, Nakazawa T, et al. Short-term effects of acupuncture on intraocular pressure in glaucoma patients: a randomized controlled trial. Explore (NY). 2012;8(4):237-241.

research.title: Acupuncture for glaucoma: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: A pilot study evaluating the effect of acupuncture on intraocular pressure and ocular perfusion in open-angle glaucoma. Results suggested a possible beneficial effect on ocular blood flow, but no significant IOP reduction was observed compared to sham.
research.periodical: Ritch R, et al. Acupuncture for glaucoma: a pilot randomized controlled trial. J Glaucoma. 2014;23(5):e1-e5.
